Greater eelpout (Lycodes esmarkii) is a benthopelagic zoarcid distributed across the cold waters of the North Atlantic, with life-history traits that reflect the constraints of a deep-water, low-temperature environment. Studies of otolith-derived growth zones indicate that individuals can attain a maximum total length of 74.5 centimeters [Li = 74.5 centimeters], representing the upper bound of somatic size for this species. Analysis of length-mass regressions further reveals that an individual reaching this asymptotic size would have a corresponding wet weight of 2391 grams [Wwi = 2391 grams], underscoring the substantial energetic commitment required to achieve maximal body dimensions under the prevailing thermal regime.

Reproductive investment in Lycodes esmarkii is tightly linked to the cold, stable temperatures characteristic of its deep-water habitat. Under experimental conditions maintained at an ambient water temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C], observations of captive broods show that the time since birth at which females attain puberty is approximately 1095 days [tp = approximately 1095 days], indicating that the onset of gonadal maturation requires roughly three years of somatic development. At this milestone, the average wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 114.6 grams [Wwp = 114.6 grams], a figure derived from the established length-to-mass conversion for this species and corresponding to a total length at puberty of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters], at which point individuals are considered primed for their first reproductive cycle.

The early life stages of the Greater eelpout are characterized by a prolonged incubation phase, a consequence of the metabolically suppressive effects of low temperature. Embryogenesis proceeds slowly at 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C], with hatching occurring after approximately 155 days [ab = approximately 155 days], a duration that is protracted relative to many shallow-water zoarcids. Upon emergence, the yolk-sac larva possesses a modest wet weight at birth of 0.0871 grams [Wwb = 0.0871 grams], a mass consistent with the small egg diameter of 5.5 millimeters from which it hatches, reflecting a lecithotrophic strategy that sustains the larva through the early period of yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding.

The species displays a notably low reproductive tempo, consistent with a long-lived, iteroparous life history. The maximum reproductive output of Lycodes esmarkii at 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C] is expressed through a low annual frequency; under these cold conditions, the daily reproduction rate is reconstructed as both a small clutch size and an extended interval between spawnings. Females produce approximately 1 to 2 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 eggs per reproductive event], and the frequency of such events is approximately 1.2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.2 clutches per year]. This slow pace of reproduction, yielding an annual output of only a few offspring, is a typical adaptation to energy-limited environments.

Longevity in Lycodes esmarkii is considerable, with the maximum recorded lifespan estimated at 14 years [am = 14 years] when maintained at a constant temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]. The delayed attainment of reproductive competence after roughly three years of development, when coupled with an extended adult phase, reinforces a strategy in which somatic persistence is favored over immediate breeding opportunities — a pattern commonly observed among cold-water ectotherms facing unpredictable spawning conditions.
